title: Simple dog portrait in cross-stitch
subtitle: A beginner-friendly 60x70 stitch portrait on 14-count Aida
excerpt: A simple dog portrait in cross-stitch is a 60-by-70 stitch piece worked on 14-count Aida. The design uses eight floss colours to suggest the face, ears, and expression of a medium-sized dog. Finished size is roughly 11 x 13 cm in the hoop.
sourceNotes: Original design for Homemade cross-stitch library. Dog portrait convention draws on historic needlework animal motifs documented in Weldon's Practical Needlework series (1880s), Internet Archive.

content.text: A simple dog portrait is a 60-by-70 stitch piece on 14-count
build the face, ears, and expression from blocks of similar tone, with a
outline on the muzzle and eye in a single strand. The finished piece is about 11 x 13 cm in a 15 cm (6 inch) hoop.
The design is worked entirely in full crosses with the back-stitch added last. No fractional stitches are needed, which makes it suitable for a stitcher who has the basic
comfortable and is ready to try a small portrait rather than a geometric or floral motif.

items.name: 14-count Aida, cream or white
items.substitutions: Pale grey gives the portrait a softer quality

content.text: Find the centre of the fabric and mount it in the hoop. Locate the centre of the chart and mark it with a pencil dot.
Begin with the largest colour block (usually the main coat colour of the dog, DMC 3782 or 3033). Work outward from the centre of that block rather than from the chart edge.
Work each colour area completely before moving to the next. The order should go from lightest to darkest: pale coat, mid coat, shadow coat, ears, muzzle, nose.

Add the eyes last in the full-cross colours, then add the back-stitch outline on the muzzle and around the eyes in a single strand of DMC 3371 (dark brown-black). Work the back-stitch after all the full crosses are done to prevent the outline stitches being pulled out of position while the nearby crosses are placed.
Wash gently in cool water and press face-down on a terry towel to dry. Display in the hoop or frame in a simple floating frame. The pale cream Aida reads well against a dark or natural wood frame.

items.symptom: The dog's eye looks like a solid block rather than a rounded shape
items.cause: The surrounding dark stitches were worked right up to the highlight stitch without leaving space for the pale reflection square.
items.fix: Place the highlight stitch first, then work the dark ring around it. Once the ring is complete, the eye should read as a circle even at arm's length.

items.symptom: The fur areas look flat rather than textured
items.cause: All the stitches in a colour area run in the same direction, which reads as a uniform block.
items.fix: Vary the direction of stitches within a fur area: work one row left-to-right, the next right-to-left. The slight tonal shift gives an impression of depth when the piece is viewed from a distance.

content.text: Try a more detailed animal next. The animals sub-category has pieces that use fractional stitches to soften curved edges on ears and noses.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

A solid outline stitch worked in a single strand along the back-stitch layer of the chart. You stitch backwards along the line one stitch at a time, each stitch finishing where the previous one started.
